clinicalPearls: A group of clonal stem cell disorders defined by ineffective haematopoiesis, producing peripheral cytopenias despite a marrow that is usually normocellular or hypercellular
Typically affects older adults, often presenting with symptomatic anaemia; neutropenia and thrombocytopenia may also occur, sometimes with recurrent infection or bleeding
The paradox of low blood counts with a busy marrow reflects intramedullary apoptosis of dysplastic precursors

Diagnosis rests on morphological dysplasia in one or more lineages, blast percentage, and cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities; ring sideroblasts and specific mutations (e.g. SF3B1) carry prognostic meaning
Risk stratification with scoring systems that weight blast count, cytogenetics, and depth of cytopenias guides both prognosis and treatment intensity

Lower-risk disease is managed supportively with transfusions, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, and iron chelation when transfusion burden is high; an isolated 5q deletion responds well to lenalidomide
Higher-risk disease is treated with hypomethylating agents, and allogeneic stem cell transplant offers the only potential cure for suitable patients
Progression to acute myeloid leukaemia is a defining risk, greatest in high-risk categories with excess blasts and adverse cytogenetics
reference.pathophysiology: MDS arises from an acquired mutation in a haematopoietic stem cell that gains a clonal growth advantage. Accumulating mutations in genes governing RNA splicing, epigenetic regulation, transcription, and signalling produce disordered maturation. Precursors are produced abundantly but undergo excessive apoptosis within the marrow, so mature cells are released ineffectively, giving cytopenias in the face of a cellular marrow. Over time the clone may acquire further mutations and expand, with rising blast counts marking transformation towards acute myeloid leukaemia. Prior chemotherapy or radiotherapy can cause therapy-related MDS, which typically carries adverse cytogenetics.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency causing megaloblastic dysplasia
Reactive dysplasia from alcohol, copper deficiency, or drugs
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count, reticulocytes, and careful blood film review for dysplastic changes
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with blast count and assessment of dysplasia and ring sideroblasts
Cytogenetic analysis and targeted molecular/next-generation sequencing panels
Serum erythropoietin level to predict response to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents
B12, folate, and copper levels to exclude reversible mimics
Flow cytometry and PNH clone testing when the picture overlaps with marrow failure
redFlags: Rising blast percentage or new adverse cytogenetics signalling transformation to acute leukaemia
Severe neutropenia with fever requiring urgent treatment for sepsis
Profound thrombocytopenia with clinically significant bleeding
Rapidly worsening pancytopenia demanding urgent haematology review and transplant assessment
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary widely by risk category: lower-risk patients may live many years with supportive care, whereas high-risk disease carries short survival and a substantial chance of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia. Allogeneic transplant is the only curative option but is limited by age and comorbidity.
pitfalls: Diagnosing MDS without excluding reversible causes of dysplasia such as B12 or folate deficiency, copper deficiency, alcohol, or recent chemotherapy
Failing to obtain cytogenetics and molecular testing, which are central to risk stratification
Undertreating iron overload in chronically transfused patients
Overlooking an isolated 5q deletion that has a favourable, targeted treatment
Missing the transition to acute leukaemia by not repeating marrow assessment when counts deteriorate
management: Risk-stratify with a validated prognostic scoring system that weights blast count, cytogenetics and depth of cytopenias to guide treatment intensity
Support lower-risk disease with red-cell transfusions and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents to improve symptomatic anaemia
Use lenalidomide for transfusion-dependent disease with an isolated 5q deletion, which responds well
Offer hypomethylating agents such as azacitidine or decitabine for higher-risk disease unsuitable for transplantation
Proceed to allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only curative option in eligible higher-risk patients
Add iron chelation therapy where a high transfusion burden causes iron overload
Treat neutropenic infection promptly with antimicrobials and give platelet transfusions for bleeding or severe thrombocytopenia
Monitor blood counts and repeat marrow assessment to detect progression towards acute myeloid leukaemia, under haematology follow-up
